ws-auth-no-origin-check.problem: Your WebSocket server accepts connections from any website. A malicious site can connect using a logged-in user's session without their knowledge.
ws-auth-no-origin-check.impact: An attacker can hijack user sessions, read private data, or perform actions as the user.
ws-auth-no-origin-check.fix: Add an origin check. Compare request.headers.get('Origin') against an allowlist before accepting the connection.

ws-auth-no-token.problem: Your WebSocket server accepts any connection without requiring an authentication token. Anyone who knows your server address can connect.
ws-auth-no-token.impact: Unauthorized users can read messages, inject data, or disrupt your service.
ws-auth-no-token.fix: Require a token in the connection URL or in the first message, validate it before processing any data.

ws-auth-no-max-size.problem: Your WebSocket server has no message size limit. A client can send a very large message to exhaust your server's memory.
ws-auth-no-max-size.impact: A single malicious client can crash your server or make it unresponsive for everyone.
ws-auth-no-max-size.fix: Set max_size in websockets.serve(), for example max_size=1_000_000 limits messages to 1 MB.

ws-auth-broadcast-no-auth.problem: Your code sends messages to every connected client without checking if each client is authorized to receive them.
ws-auth-broadcast-no-auth.impact: Sensitive messages may be delivered to unauthenticated or unauthorized users.
ws-auth-broadcast-no-auth.fix: Maintain a separate set of authenticated clients and only broadcast to those.

ws-auth-msg-not-validated.problem: Your WebSocket handler processes incoming messages without checking their size or format. Malformed or oversized input can cause crashes or unexpected behavior.
ws-auth-msg-not-validated.impact: Attackers can send crafted messages to trigger errors, bypass logic, or exhaust resources.
ws-auth-msg-not-validated.fix: Check message length and parse/validate the format (e.g. JSON schema) before processing.

injection-shell-true.problem: Running a command with shell=True means the shell interprets the entire command string. If any part comes from user input, the user can inject arbitrary shell commands.
injection-shell-true.impact: Full remote code execution. An attacker can run any command on your server.
injection-shell-true.fix: Pass the command as a list of arguments and remove shell=True. Example: subprocess.run(['ls', '-l', path]).

injection-subprocess-shell-true.problem: subprocess.Popen with shell=True has the same risk as subprocess.run with shell=True: user input embedded in the command string can be exploited.
injection-subprocess-shell-true.impact: Full remote code execution on the server.
injection-subprocess-shell-true.fix: Pass a list of arguments instead: subprocess.Popen(['cmd', 'arg1', arg2]).

injection-os-system.problem: os.system() passes its argument directly to the shell. Any user-controlled content in that argument can inject arbitrary commands.
injection-os-system.impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the server.
injection-os-system.fix: Replace os.system() with subprocess.run() using a list of arguments and no shell=True.

injection-eval.problem: eval() executes the string it receives as Python code. If that string includes any user-provided content, the user can run arbitrary code.
injection-eval.impact: Complete system compromise — the attacker can read files, open network connections, or destroy data.
injection-eval.fix: Avoid eval() entirely. Use a safe parser or restrict input to a known set of values.

injection-exec.problem: exec() is the same as eval() but also supports multi-statement code blocks. It executes the given string as Python code.
injection-exec.impact: Complete system compromise — same risk as eval().
injection-exec.fix: Avoid exec() entirely. If you need dynamic behavior, use a restricted DSL or configuration format instead.

injection-path-traversal-open.problem: Opening a file at a path that includes a variable could allow path traversal. An attacker may pass '../../../etc/passwd' to escape your intended directory.
injection-path-traversal-open.impact: An attacker can read or overwrite arbitrary files on the system.
injection-path-traversal-open.fix: Use pathlib.Path.resolve() and verify the resolved path starts with your intended base directory before opening.

injection-sql-f-string.problem: Building a SQL query with an f-string embeds variables directly into the query text. If a variable contains SQL syntax, it changes the query structure.
injection-sql-f-string.impact: An attacker can read, modify, or delete any data in your database, or execute admin commands.
injection-sql-f-string.fix: Use parameterized queries: cursor.execute('SELECT ... WHERE id = %s', (user_id,)).

injection-sql-concat.problem: Concatenating strings to build a SQL query is vulnerable to SQL injection for the same reason as f-strings: user input can alter the query structure.
injection-sql-concat.impact: Full database compromise — an attacker can exfiltrate, modify, or destroy all data.
injection-sql-concat.fix: Use parameterized queries: cursor.execute('SELECT ... WHERE name = %s', (name,)).

injection-js-eval.problem: JavaScript eval() executes its argument as code. User-controlled content passed to eval() gives the attacker full script execution in the page context.
injection-js-eval.impact: XSS, session theft, DOM manipulation, exfiltration of cookies and tokens.
injection-js-eval.fix: Never pass user input to eval(). Use JSON.parse() for data, or rethink the logic that requires eval().

injection-js-innerhtml.problem: Assigning a variable to innerHTML causes the browser to parse it as HTML and execute any embedded scripts. If the variable contains user input, it is an XSS vulnerability.
injection-js-innerhtml.impact: An attacker can inject scripts that steal session tokens, redirect users, or deface the page.
injection-js-innerhtml.fix: Use textContent instead of innerHTML. If you must insert HTML, sanitize the input with DOMPurify first.

crypto-md5.problem: MD5 is a broken hash algorithm. It is computationally feasible to find collisions, and preimage attacks are practical for short inputs.
crypto-md5.impact: Password hashes can be cracked quickly; checksums can be forged.
crypto-md5.fix: Use hashlib.sha256() for general hashing. For passwords, use bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2.

crypto-sha1.problem: SHA-1 is considered weak. Chosen-prefix collision attacks have been demonstrated, and it is deprecated by NIST.
crypto-sha1.impact: Digital signatures and certificates using SHA-1 can be forged.

crypto-hardcoded-secret.problem: A secret key, token, or password is hardcoded as a string literal in the source code. Anyone with access to the repository or binary can extract it.
crypto-hardcoded-secret.impact: Full compromise of the service or account protected by that credential.
crypto-hardcoded-secret.fix: Move credentials to environment variables or a secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or .env files excluded from version control.

crypto-weak-random.problem: random.random() uses a Mersenne Twister which is not cryptographically secure. Its output can be predicted from a few observed values.
crypto-weak-random.impact: Tokens, nonces, and session IDs generated this way can be guessed by an attacker.
crypto-weak-random.fix: Use the secrets module: secrets.token_hex(32) for tokens, secrets.randbelow(n) for integers.

crypto-pickle-load.problem: pickle.loads() can execute arbitrary Python code during deserialization. It is not safe to unpickle data from an untrusted source.
crypto-pickle-load.impact: Remote code execution — an attacker can craft a pickle payload to run any code on your server.
crypto-pickle-load.fix: Never deserialize pickled data from untrusted sources. Use JSON or a schema-validated format like msgpack.

crypto-yaml-load.problem: yaml.load() without a Loader argument or with the default Loader can instantiate arbitrary Python objects from the YAML document.
crypto-yaml-load.impact: Remote code execution if the YAML is sourced from user input or an untrusted file.
crypto-yaml-load.fix: Replace yaml.load(x) with yaml.safe_load(x), which only deserializes basic Python types.

crypto-md5-js.problem: MD5 is a weak hash algorithm that should not be used for security purposes.
crypto-md5-js.impact: Checksums can be forged; any data integrity or authentication relying on MD5 is unreliable.
crypto-md5-js.fix: Use crypto.createHash('sha256') or crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', ...) for Web Crypto API.

crypto-jwt-none-alg.problem: Allowing the 'none' algorithm in JWT verification disables signature checking entirely. Any token will be accepted as valid.
crypto-jwt-none-alg.impact: An attacker can forge tokens for any user, including admins, without knowing any secret.
crypto-jwt-none-alg.fix: Remove 'none' from the algorithms array. Only allow the specific algorithm your tokens are signed with, e.g. ['HS256'].

xss-dangerously-set-html.problem: dangerouslySetInnerHTML tells React to inject raw HTML into the DOM, bypassing React's automatic escaping. If the value contains user input, scripts can be injected.
xss-dangerously-set-html.impact: XSS — an attacker can steal session cookies, redirect users, or deface the page.
xss-dangerously-set-html.fix: Sanitize the HTML with DOMPurify before passing it to dangerouslySetInnerHTML, or restructure the component to avoid raw HTML injection.

xss-document-write.problem: document.write() appends raw content to the document. Content that includes user input can inject scripts.
xss-document-write.impact: XSS — same impact as innerHTML assignment.
xss-document-write.fix: Use DOM methods like createElement and appendChild, or textContent for plain text.

xss-direct-innerhtml.problem: Assigning to innerHTML parses the value as HTML and executes embedded scripts. Any user-controlled value is an XSS risk.
xss-direct-innerhtml.impact: Script injection, session theft, page defacement.
xss-direct-innerhtml.fix: Use textContent for plain text. Sanitize with DOMPurify if you must insert HTML.

xss-href-javascript.problem: Setting href to a javascript: URL causes the browser to execute JavaScript when the link is clicked. If the URL comes from user input, it is XSS.
xss-href-javascript.impact: Code execution in the page context on click — session theft or malicious actions.
xss-href-javascript.fix: Validate all href values against an allowlist of protocols (https:, mailto:) and reject javascript: URLs.

xss-set-attribute-onevent.problem: Setting an on* attribute (onclick, onerror, etc.) via setAttribute injects an event handler. If the value is user-controlled, this is XSS.
xss-set-attribute-onevent.impact: Arbitrary script execution triggered by user interaction.
xss-set-attribute-onevent.fix: Use addEventListener instead of setAttribute for event handlers. Never set on* attributes with user-controlled values.

llm-fake-pandas-method.problem: This method does not exist in the pandas library. It was likely suggested by an AI assistant that hallucinated a plausible-sounding but nonexistent API.
llm-fake-pandas-method.impact: The code will raise AttributeError at runtime.
llm-fake-pandas-method.fix: Check the official pandas documentation for the correct method name and signature.

llm-fake-react-hook.problem: useFetch and useDebounce are not part of React's core API. They are frequently hallucinated by AI code generators as if they were built-in hooks.
llm-fake-react-hook.impact: The code will fail at runtime because these hooks do not exist in React.
llm-fake-react-hook.fix: Install a library that provides them (e.g. react-use, usehooks-ts) or implement them yourself. Check the React documentation for the list of built-in hooks.

bug-async-without-await.problem: This async function never uses await, so it runs synchronously and the async wrapper adds no benefit.
bug-async-without-await.impact: The function still returns a Promise, which callers must handle, but the async keyword is misleading and hides the actual execution flow.
bug-async-without-await.fix: Remove the async keyword if the function has no asynchronous operations, or add the missing await before the async call inside the function body.

bug-loose-equality.problem: The == operator performs type coercion, which can produce surprising results. For example, 0 == false is true and '' == 0 is true.
bug-loose-equality.impact: Logic bugs where values that should be different are treated as equal, leading to incorrect branching or data processing.
bug-loose-equality.fix: Use === (strict equality) instead of ==. It checks both value and type without coercion.

bug-missing-await.problem: An async function is called but its returned Promise is assigned without await. The variable holds a Promise object, not the resolved value.
bug-missing-await.impact: You will be working with a Promise instead of the data you expected, causing errors or silent wrong behavior downstream.
bug-missing-await.fix: Add await before the async function call: const result = await myAsyncFn().

bug-dict-get-no-default.problem: dict.get(key) returns None when the key is missing. If the caller does not check for None, subsequent operations on the result will fail.
bug-dict-get-no-default.impact: AttributeError or TypeError at runtime when code tries to use a None value as if it were a real object.
bug-dict-get-no-default.fix: Provide a default: dict.get(key, default_value). Choose a sensible default (e.g. 0, [], or an empty string) or explicitly handle the None case.

bug-mutable-default-arg.problem: Default argument values are evaluated once when the function is defined, not each time it is called. A mutable default like [] is shared across all calls.
bug-mutable-default-arg.impact: Mutations inside the function persist across calls, causing state to leak between unrelated invocations.
bug-mutable-default-arg.fix: Use None as the default and create a new mutable object inside the function: def f(items=None): if items is None: items = []

bug-off-by-one-range.problem: range(1, len(arr)) skips index 0, so the first element of the array is never processed.
bug-off-by-one-range.impact: The first item is silently ignored, which can produce wrong totals, missed validations, or incomplete processing.
bug-off-by-one-range.fix: Use range(len(arr)) to start from index 0, or range(0, len(arr)) to be explicit.

bug-unused-exception.problem: A bare except: pass or except Exception: pass silently swallows all errors without logging or re-raising them.
bug-unused-exception.impact: Real failures are hidden, making debugging very difficult. The program continues in a potentially invalid state.
bug-unused-exception.fix: At minimum, log the exception: except Exception as e: logger.error(e). Re-raise if you cannot handle it gracefully.

bug-promise-not-awaited.problem: A Promise-returning function is called but its result is not awaited or handled with .then()/.catch(). The Promise runs in the background with no way to react to success or failure.
bug-promise-not-awaited.impact: Errors are silently swallowed and success side-effects may run after the surrounding code has already completed.
bug-promise-not-awaited.fix: Add await before the call in an async context, or chain .then() and .catch() to handle the result explicitly.

bug-string-concat-int.problem: Adding a string and an integer with + raises a TypeError in Python. Python does not auto-coerce types during concatenation.
bug-string-concat-int.impact: The program crashes at runtime with TypeError: can only concatenate str (not 'int') to str.
bug-string-concat-int.fix: Explicitly convert the integer to a string: str(num) + text, or use an f-string: f'{text}{num}'.

bug-array-includes-NaN.problem: Array.prototype.includes() uses SameValueZero comparison, which means [NaN].includes(NaN) correctly returns true — but Array.prototype.indexOf(NaN) always returns -1 because it uses strict equality where NaN !== NaN.
bug-array-includes-NaN.impact: Code that uses indexOf to check for NaN will always fail to find it, producing wrong results silently.
bug-array-includes-NaN.fix: Use Number.isNaN() to check for NaN, or use Array.prototype.includes() instead of indexOf when searching for NaN.

bug-react-key-missing.problem: React requires each element in a list to have a unique key prop so it can efficiently update the DOM. Without it, React must re-render entire lists on every change.
bug-react-key-missing.impact: Slow re-renders, incorrect component state after list updates, and React console warnings in development.
bug-react-key-missing.fix: Add a unique key prop to the outermost element returned from map(): arr.map(item => <Component key={item.id} />).

bug-typeof-null-object.problem: In JavaScript, typeof null === 'object' is true, which is a historical language bug. Checking typeof x === 'object' without also checking x !== null will incorrectly treat null as an object.
bug-typeof-null-object.impact: Code that relies on this check to confirm an object exists will silently pass null through, causing errors later when properties are accessed.
bug-typeof-null-object.fix: Add an explicit null check: typeof x === 'object' && x !== null. Better yet, use a dedicated type-guard function.

llm-deprecated-pandas-append.problem: DataFrame.append() was removed in pandas 2.0. Code using it was likely generated by an AI assistant trained on older pandas documentation.
llm-deprecated-pandas-append.impact: The code raises AttributeError at runtime on pandas 2.0 and later.
llm-deprecated-pandas-append.fix: Replace df.append(other) with pd.concat([df, other], ignore_index=True).

llm-deprecated-react-lifecycle.problem: componentWillMount is deprecated in React 16.3 and removed in React 18. AI code generators frequently produce it because it appeared in older tutorials.
llm-deprecated-react-lifecycle.impact: The component will fail in strict mode, and the code will break entirely in React 18.
llm-deprecated-react-lifecycle.fix: Move initialization logic to componentDidMount or, better yet, convert to a functional component using useEffect.

llm-fake-numpy-fast-dot.problem: np.fast_dot does not exist in NumPy. It was hallucinated by an AI assistant as a plausible-sounding performance variant of np.dot.
llm-fake-numpy-fast-dot.fix: Use np.dot(a, b) or the @ operator (a @ b) for matrix multiplication.

llm-fake-pandas-clean-csv.problem: df.to_clean_csv() does not exist in pandas. It was hallucinated by an AI assistant. The real method is to_csv() with options.
llm-fake-pandas-clean-csv.fix: Use df.to_csv('file.csv', index=False) to write a clean CSV without the index column.

logic-conditional-side-effect.problem: A side-effecting statement appears directly inside an if without a block. This is fragile and may indicate missing braces or an accidental guard condition.
logic-conditional-side-effect.impact: Refactoring the condition or adding another statement can silently change which code is guarded by the if.
logic-conditional-side-effect.fix: Always use explicit braces for if blocks, even for single-statement bodies: if (cond) { statement; }

logic-fetch-no-error-check.problem: fetch() does not throw on HTTP errors like 404 or 500 — it only throws on network failures. Using response.json() directly without checking response.ok silently processes error responses.
logic-fetch-no-error-check.impact: Your code may process an error page's HTML as if it were valid JSON, causing cryptic parse errors or incorrect data.
logic-fetch-no-error-check.fix: Check response.ok before consuming the body: if (!response.ok) throw new Error(response.statusText); const data = await response.json();

logic-file-not-closed.problem: Opening a file with open() outside a with statement requires manually calling .close(). If an exception occurs before .close(), the file descriptor leaks.
logic-file-not-closed.impact: File descriptor leaks can cause the program to crash with 'too many open files' errors under load.
logic-file-not-closed.fix: Use a with statement: with open(path) as f: ... — it guarantees the file is closed even if an exception is raised.

logic-json-parse-no-try.problem: JSON.parse() throws a SyntaxError if the input is not valid JSON. If the call is not wrapped in try/catch, a malformed response will crash the application.
logic-json-parse-no-try.impact: Unhandled exception from a single bad API response can crash the entire page or service.
logic-json-parse-no-try.fix: Wrap in try/catch: try { const data = JSON.parse(text); } catch { /* handle invalid JSON */ }

logic-lock-without-unlock.problem: Calling lock.acquire() without a try/finally block means the lock will not be released if an exception is raised in the protected code.
logic-lock-without-unlock.impact: A deadlock will occur — other threads waiting on the lock will block forever.
logic-lock-without-unlock.fix: Use a with statement: with lock: ... — it acquires and releases automatically, even on exceptions.

logic-unhandled-promise-rejection.problem: A .then() chain without a .catch() will silently swallow any rejection. In Node.js, unhandled rejections can crash the process in newer versions.
logic-unhandled-promise-rejection.impact: Errors are hidden and the application can reach an invalid state with no indication of what went wrong.
logic-unhandled-promise-rejection.fix: Always append .catch(err => ...) to promise chains, or use async/await with try/catch.

quality-any-type.problem: TypeScript's any type disables all type checking for that value. Using it defeats the purpose of TypeScript and makes the code as unsafe as plain JavaScript.
quality-any-type.impact: Type errors that TypeScript would normally catch at compile time will become runtime crashes.
quality-any-type.fix: Replace any with the specific type, unknown (for truly unknown data), or a generic type parameter.

quality-console-log-prod.problem: console.log() statements left in production code pollute the browser console and may accidentally expose sensitive data to users.
quality-console-log-prod.impact: Sensitive information (tokens, user data) can be leaked to the browser console. The console fills with noise that hides real errors.
quality-console-log-prod.fix: Remove console.log before committing, or replace with a structured logger that can be disabled in production.

quality-long-function.problem: Functions that span many lines are harder to understand, test, and maintain. They often do too many things at once.
quality-long-function.impact: Bugs are harder to find, tests are harder to write, and changes in one part of the function can unexpectedly affect other parts.
quality-long-function.fix: Split the function into smaller, focused helper functions. Aim for functions under 40-50 lines that each do one thing.

quality-magic-number.problem: A numeric literal with no obvious meaning is embedded directly in code. Future readers cannot tell what the number represents or why it has that specific value.
quality-magic-number.impact: Maintenance becomes error-prone: the same magic number may be duplicated, and changing it requires finding every occurrence.
quality-magic-number.fix: Extract the number to a named constant at the top of the file or module: MAX_RETRIES = 3.

quality-no-docstring.problem: A public Python function has no docstring to explain what it does, what parameters it accepts, and what it returns.
quality-no-docstring.impact: Other developers (and tools like help() or IDEs) cannot understand the function's purpose without reading its implementation.
quality-no-docstring.fix: Add a docstring immediately after the def line: """Brief description. Args: x: ... Returns: ..."""

quality-no-jsdoc.problem: An exported TypeScript function has no JSDoc comment, so its purpose, parameters, and return value are not documented.
quality-no-jsdoc.impact: IDEs cannot show hover documentation, and other developers must read the implementation to understand how to use the function.
quality-no-jsdoc.fix: Add a JSDoc comment above the function: /** Description. @param name - what it does. @returns what comes back. */

quality-todo-comment.problem: A TODO comment marks incomplete or deferred work. If not tracked elsewhere, it may never be resolved and will age into misleading technical debt.
quality-todo-comment.impact: Unresolved TODOs accumulate, making the codebase harder to trust. They can indicate missing validations or incomplete features.
quality-todo-comment.fix: Either fix the issue now, create a tracked ticket and reference it in the comment (TODO #123), or remove the comment if it is no longer relevant.

quality-too-many-args.problem: A function with many positional arguments is hard to call correctly — callers must remember the exact order and meaning of each argument.
quality-too-many-args.impact: Arguments are easily passed in the wrong order, causing subtle bugs that are hard to debug.
quality-too-many-args.fix: Group related arguments into a dataclass or dict, or use keyword-only arguments: def f(*, name, value, ...).
